title: Structured Prompts to Complete a Task
summary: Students learn the Goal-Context-Format prompt structure, use it to complete a defined task on a teacher-operated tool, judge whether the task was completed, and make one adjustment to complete it more fully.
objectives: Use a structured prompt to complete a defined task with an AI tool.
Describe the input structure used and whether the task was completed.
Adjust the prompt once to complete the task more fully.

sections.heading: Structured Prompts to Complete a Task
body: Ask an AI tool a vague question and you get a vague answer. Learn to structure your prompt and you can actually get a task done. Today you learn the trick: **Goal, Context, Format**.

sections.heading: I can…
items: I can write a structured prompt with a clear goal, context and format.
I can say whether the task was completed and why.
I can improve my prompt once to complete the task more fully.

terms.definition: The instruction you give an AI tool.
A prompt with a clear goal, context and format.
What you want the tool to do.
The details the tool needs to do it.
How you want the answer to look.

sections.heading: Goal, Context, Format
body: A vague prompt like 'tell me about the desert' leaves the tool guessing. A [[structured prompt]] tells it exactly what to do.
**Goal**: what you want. **Context**: the details it needs. **Format**: how the answer should look. Together they make the task far more likely to be completed.

sections.label: The shape of a structured prompt
sections.heading: One prompt, three slots
sections.altText: A single bar split into three labelled slots — Goal, Context and Format — which together make a prompt the tool can act on.

parts.label: Goal
parts.detail: What you want it to do

parts.label: Context
parts.detail: What it needs to know first

sections.result: A prompt the tool can act on
sections.caption: Leave a slot empty and the tool fills it with a guess of its own. **Format is the one most often left out**, and it is why an answer comes back in the wrong shape.

sections.heading: Check, then improve
body: Once you get an output, compare it to the task. Did it do everything you asked? If not, change one thing in your prompt and try again.
Two safety rules: never put personal data in a prompt, and always verify the answer - a confident output can still be wrong.

sections.label: Let's try it - hands-on
sections.heading: Let's try it - hands-on
body: Write a structured prompt for a real task, judge whether it completed the task, and improve it once.
items: Underline what 'complete' means for your task.

Watch the teacher run it on the approved tool.
Judge whether the task was completed.
Adjust your prompt once and verify the output.

items: Which part of the structure helped most?
How did you know the task was or was not complete?

Write one safety rule you used today.

worksheet.title: Week 3 - Core - Worksheet | Structured Prompts to Complete a Task

questions.prompt: Maya's task: give Grade 6 students exactly three bullet points on our school's recycling rules. She typed the prompt 'Tell me about recycling.' The tool returned six long paragraphs about recycling around the world. Which single adjustment does the most to complete Maya's task?

options.text: Run the same prompt again, because the tool gives a different answer each time.
Add 'make it shorter' to the end of the prompt she already used.
Rewrite it as 'Summarise our school's recycling rules for Grade 6 students in exactly three bullet points.'
Paste the six paragraphs back in and ask the tool whether they are correct.

feedback.correct: That rewrite supplies the goal (summarise the rules), the context (our school, Grade 6) and the format (exactly three bullets), so the tool can actually complete the task.
feedback.incorrect: The output missed the task on goal, context and format at once, so the fix has to put all three in - shortening or re-running a vague prompt still leaves the tool guessing.

questions.prompt: Omar is writing a prompt for a class task. Match each line he wrote to the part of a structured prompt it belongs to.

left.text: Write a packing list for our Grade 6 desert field trip.
The trip is one day in February and we walk for two hours in the sun.
Give it as a numbered list of eight items, each under six words.
I am Omar Al Hosani, Class 6B, phone 050 ...

right.text: Goal - what you want the tool to do
Context - the details the tool needs
Format - how the answer should look
Leave this out - personal data never goes in a prompt

feedback.correct: Goal, context and format each do a different job, and personal details do none of them - they only put you at risk.
feedback.incorrect: Ask what each line is for: the goal names the task, the context gives the tool the facts it needs, the format shapes the answer, and a name or phone number belongs in none of them.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of today's task in the order the lesson used them.

items.text: Write down exactly what 'complete' would mean for this task.
Write the prompt with a goal, context and format.
Watch the prompt run on the approved tool.
Compare the output with the task and judge whether it was completed.
Change one thing in the prompt, run it again and verify the new output.

feedback.correct: Deciding what 'complete' means first is what lets you judge the output honestly and choose a useful adjustment afterwards.
feedback.incorrect: You cannot judge an output before you have decided what completing the task looks like, and the adjustment only makes sense after you have seen where the first output fell short.

questions.prompt: True or false: if the output is long, well written and sounds confident, that is enough to show the task was completed.

feedback.correct: Right - you judge an output against what the task asked for, because a confident answer can still be incomplete or wrong.
feedback.incorrect: Sounding right is not the same as being right: check the output against the task you set, not against how polished it reads.

questions.prompt: The task was: three bullet points on the water cycle for Grade 6, each under twelve words. The output came back with five bullets, two of them about twenty words long, and one bullet states something the science textbook says is wrong. Which of these show the task was NOT completed? Choose all that apply.

options.text: There are five bullets when the task asked for three.
Two of the bullets run to about twenty words.
One bullet is wrong when checked against the science textbook.
The answer is set out as bullet points instead of a paragraph.
The bullets are written in a friendly tone, which nobody asked for.

feedback.correct: Number, length and accuracy were all part of the task, so each of those three misses counts - and a wrong fact fails the task even when the format is perfect.
feedback.incorrect: Compare the output with the task line by line: bullets were requested and the tone was never specified, so only the count, the length and the wrong fact are genuine misses.

formative.targets: Directly checks 'uses AI tools with structured prompts to complete tasks'
formative.check: Task-completion log: structured prompt, output, 'task complete?' + one adjustment
formative.successCriteria: Completes the task using a structured prompt and records one adjustment that improved completion.
